# Introduction

Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to alter the fundamental
design and experience of work. The Job Characteristics Model (JCM;
Hackman & Oldham, 1975, 1976) proposes that core job characteristics
shape critical psychological states and, ultimately, important employee
outcomes. Emerging research suggests that digitization may substantially
alter these characteristics. For example, digital technologies may
automate repetitive tasks, but they may also fragment work, limit skill
use, or diminish employees’ sense of ownership over their work. Arora
and Garg’s (2025) review of meaningful work in the digital age
identifies autonomy, skill variety, feedback, task significance, and
task identity as job characteristics affected by workplace digitization.
As AI’s role in the design and performance of work grows it is important
to understand how employees engage with the technology.\
Conceptualizing and measuring employee AI use is challenging. Existing
research operationalizes AI use in terms of the extent or intensity it
is used to perform work. For example, Zhang et al. (2026) measure AI
usage with items assessing the degree to which employees use AI in
carrying out their job functions. Increasing AI integration may alter
employees’ routines, role boundaries, autonomy, and skills, suggesting
that the potential impact of AI use likely goes beyond frequency or
intensity. Two employees could report similarly high levels of AI use
while interacting with the technology in fundamentally different ways.
One employee may primarily use AI to automate routine administrative
work, another may use it to generate and refine ideas, and still another
may engage with AI iteratively as a source of expertise or cognitive
challenge. Accordingly, understanding AI-enabled work may require
measures that capture how they incorporate AI into their work.Callari
and Puppione (2025) provide one framework for distinguish forms of AI
use. Drawing on qualitative data from employees using Microsoft 365
Copilot, they identified three ideal types of AI users
Efficiency-Seeking, Pragmatic Integrators, and Collaborative Optimizers.
These ideal types imply qualitatively different relationships between AI
and features of work including autonomy, skill utilization, cognitive
effort, and decision-making. The Callari and Puppione (2025) framework
suggests that AI use is not a uniform behavior but rather is best
considered multidimensional.Yet, translating qualitative ideal types
into quantitative measures presents a challenge. Ideal types represent
recurring patterns of behavior and experience, but they do not
necessarily correspond to distinct psychological constructs. Additional
work is needed to determine whether AI user types such as those
presented by Callari and Puppione (2025) can be measured with survey
items. Interestingly, the measurement of AI use is potentially enriched
by recent technological developments. For a long time, the scale
development process has relied on the efforts of researchers and
subject-matter experts to turn construct definitions to survey items
measuring the construct. Now, generative AI now provides tools for
producing surveys that measure constructs from idea generation to item
testing. However, the question of whether survey items produced by
generative AI can properly measure constructs. The present study is an
exploratory comparison of three approaches to developing items intended
to assess employees’ orientations toward workplace AI use. Specifically,
we compare items generated through (a) ChatGPT based on Callari and
Puppione’s (2025) ideal AI user types, (b) AI Genie, and (c)
industrial-organizational psychology subject-matter experts. We evaluate
the internal consistency and underlying factor structure of each item
set. In doing so, this study has two primary objectives: first, to
provide evidence regarding whether qualitatively derived forms of
human–AI interaction can be operationalized as quantitative constructs,
and second, to examine whether different approaches to item generation
yield comparable representations of those constructs. More broadly,
establishing how employees differ in their use of AI represents an
important step toward understanding how AI may reshape established
features of job design and the psychological experience of work.

>Research Question: Does one instrument development procedure emerge as better?

# Method

## Participants

UW-Stout students who are employed

## Measures

JCM original measure: @hackman1975development 


## Procedure

### ChatGPT

The prompt was: "I need your help with generating a tentative
list of survey items. I am reading the attached paper for the third time
[the @callari2025meaningful paper]. I am interested in the three AI
user ideal types and the survey items that could be generated to measure
an employee's propensity toward one type or another."

### AI--GENIE

### SME

The traditional items were generated by paper authors. The three adopter types were treated as individual constructs, with definitions provided by @callari2025meaningful. An initial list of 57 candidate items was reduced to 16 through consensus evaluation of item clarity and content domain coverage. 

# Results

Exploratory factor analyses (EFAs) were conducted separately for each of
the three item sets: ChatGPT--generated, subject-matter expert
(SME)--generated, and AI Genie--generated. One, two, and three-factor
solutions were estimated for each item set using maximum likelihood
estimation and an oblique Quartimin rotation. Following @hu1999cutoff's guidelines, model fit was evaluated using multiple indicators
including the chi-square test of model fit, root mean square error of
approximation (RMSEA), comparative fit index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis index
(TLI), and standardized root mean square residual (SRMR). Across all
three item sets, model fit improved significantly as additional factors
were extracted. Parallel analysis, however, suggested different levels
of dimensionality across the item sets, with a one-factor solution for
the AI Genie and SME item sets and a two-factor solution for the ChatGPT
item set. Because the item pools were constructed to represent three
conceptual domains, the three-factor solutions are discussed here to
evaluate the pattern of item loadings and correspondence between the
intended and emergent factor structures. The three-factor solution for
the AI Genie-generated items demonstrated substantially better fit
compared to the one- and two-factor models, χ²(150) = 207.64, p = .001,
RMSEA = .064, 90% CI \[.041, .084\], CFI = .960, TLI = .944, and SRMR =
.036. Item loading patterns provided partial evidence of a clear
three-factor structure. Factor 1 was defined by four EF items and two PI
items: GENIE_EF_2 (.643), GENIE_EF_3 (.853), GENIE_EF_5 (.769),
GENIE_EF_7 (.760), GENIE_PI_1 (.702), and GENIE_PI_4 (.744). The second
factor included items from all groups of items with significant loadings
occurring for GENIE_PI_2 (.804), GENIE_PI_3 (.868), GENIE_PI_6 (.670),
GENIE_PI_7 (.658), GENIE_CO_3 (.728), GENIE_CO_4 (.625), and GENIE_CO_5
(.693). Additionally, items GENIE_EF_1, GENIE_EF_6, and GENIE_PI_5, had
significant cross loadings on Factors 1 and 2. Compared to Factors 1 and
2, Factor 3 was weakly defined. GENIE_CO_6 demonstrated the clearest
loading on this factor (.562), whereas GENIE_CO_1 had a smaller loading
of (.388). GENIE-EF_4 which significantly loaded onto Factor 2 had a
significant negative loading on Factor 3 (-.310). Factor 1 and Factor 2
had a significant correlation (r = .762, p \< .05), whereas the
correlations of Factor 3 with Factors 1 (r = .295) and 2 (r = .289) did
not approach statistical significance. Overall, the three-factor model
demonstrated relatively good fit, the loading pattern suggests two
somewhat clear factors with item cross loadings and an ambiguous third
factor.\

The three-factor solution for the SME-generated items demonstrated the
strongest overall model fit of the three item-generation approaches,
χ²(150) = 183.17, p = .034, RMSEA = .048, 90% CI \[.015, .071\], CFI =
.962, TLI = .947, and SRMR = .050. Factor 1 was defined by PI items,
including SME_PI_1 (.521) and SME_PI_2 (.597), SME_PI_4 (.656), SME_PI_6
(.595), and SME_PI_7 (.564), as well as SME_CO_1 (.629) and SME_CO_5
(.407). Additionally, four items including SME_ES_3 (-.559), SME_ES_5
(-.574), and SME_ES_7 (-.630) loaded negatively onto this factor. Items
SME_ES_1 (.740) and SME_PI_3 (.724) loaded mostly strongly on Factor 2,
with SME_ES_6 exhibiting a more modest loading (.351). Factor 3 was
primarily defined by SME_PI_5 (.790) and several CO items, including
SME_CO_2 (.402), SME_CO_3 (.553), SME_CO_4 (.411), SME_CO_6 (.672), and
SME_CO_7 (.584). SME_ES_4 exhibited loadings on both Factor 1 (-.320)
and Factor 3 (.388), while SME_ES_2 did not load strongly on any single
factor. All three factors were significantly correlated at the 5% level
threshold (p \< .05) . Factor 1 correlated .441 with Factor 2 and .635
with Factor 3, while Factors 2 and 3 correlated .458. Overall, the
three-factor model provided strong fit, although the like the AI_Genie
items, loadings did not create three distinct item groupings.\
Like the other two item sets, model fit improved as additional factors
were extracted for the ChatGPT-generated items. The three-factor model
provided the best fit of the models examined for the ChatGPT-Generated
items, χ²(207) = 347.09, p \< .001, RMSEA = .084, 90% CI \[.068, .099\],
CFI = .879, TLI = .838, and SRMR = .053. Despite this improvement, the
additional indicators of model fit (RMSEA, CFI, and TLI) indicated
relatively worse fit than the three-factor solutions for the SME and
AI_Genie models.\

Nonetheless, the three-factor solution revealed several interpretable
item loadings. Factor 1 was primarily defined by ES items, including
chat_ES_1 (.472), chat_ES_3 (.769), chat_ES_6 (.680), and chat_ES_8
(.453), and chat_PI_3 (.495) which also had a significant negative
cross-loading with Factor 3 (-.303). Factor 2 was defined by the PI and
CO items. PI item loadings on Factor 2 included chat_PI_1 (.751),
chat_PI_4 (.765), chat_PI_6 (.600), chat_PI_7 (.601), and chat_PI_8
(.464). All eight CO items loaded most strongly on Factor 2, with
loadings ranging from .490 to .864. Finally, Factor 3 was defined by a
handful of ES items, including chat_ES_4 (.520), chat_ES_5 (.650), and
chat_ES_8 (.490). Notably, chat_ES_8 cross-loaded on Factors 1 (.453)
and 3 (.490), while chat_ES_7 did not load strongly on any factor.
Factors 1 and 2 were significantly correlated (r = .477, p \< .05),
while Factor 3 was did not have a significant correlation with Factor 1
(r = -.029) or Factor 2 (r = -.146). Taken together, these results
suggest that the ChatGPT-generated items exhibited meaningful
multidimensionality, but the observed structure did not cleanly produce
loadings indicating three distinct factors. Additionally, the
ChatGPT-generated items demonstrated worse model fit than the
corresponding SME and AI Genie item sets.

# Discussion

1. methodological contribution -- EGAs plus EFAs, empirical vs semantic
  + cross--loading clearing up
2. theoretical contribution (AI adopter type)
  + distinct types vs different gradients of expertise (degree of AI collaboration)
  
## Limitations

Sample size as well as well as sample characteristics (degree of AI integration within workplace)
